title: How a solver checks that 600 AI-coded Roblox puzzle rooms are beatable, and three places it still went wrong
author: icygnum
selftext:
My son designed the levels for a small web game where you flick a marshmallow onto a campfire. I ported it to Roblox in 3D, on Linux with Rojo and no Studio. Most of the Luau was written by AI coding assistants in my editor; I review and test every change. The AI did not design the levels. My son did.



600 rooms is too many to play by hand, so a solver plays them. A room ships only if:

\- the solver beats it within 3 flicks

\- the win isn't fragile (a small change in angle or power doesn't break it)

\- the stored win replays and passes verification

\- the fire is visible in the opening frame



A test suite replays every stored win. The full run is about 3,400 tests, all passing.



Where it still went wrong:



\- The camera. After a camera change, mouse drag felt inverted on PC while the phone was fine. I pinned it with 17 tests that check what the player sees, and a failing one gets fixed in the source, never in the test.

\- "Beatable" is not "playable". Every room passed, yet about 19 of 95 players in an ad test stopped at room 9. After a landing the fire left the frame (51% of landing spots there, 35% in the next room). The solver doesn't need to see the fire; a player does. I added a camera pan to the fire and a one-time hint. The new data isn't in yet, so I'm not calling it fixed.

\- Known leftovers. Tests flag floor fans that let a flight drift along the floor forever in 3 rooms, and one gear that squeezes the marshmallow up to 8 px into a wall in 8 rooms. They are listed as exceptions; Try again is the workaround.



Next: Christmas worlds open Sunday 8 Nov (Gingerbread Bakery, sticky icing), then a new world each week. There's also a Party Race for up to 8 friends. It's 16+ for now.



How do you verify AI-written gameplay code beyond unit tests?
